title: Work Whiplash
author: Graham, Molly
summary: Molly Graham, founder of Glue Club, names a pattern she calls "work whiplash" — the morale-destroying experience of executing against a goal only to discover leadership changed direction without telling the people doing the work. Unlike the difficulty of hard work itself, whiplash is the product of a gap between what leaders know and what employees know — a gap that kills motivation by signaling that individual effort does not matter. Graham identifies the most common forms: undisclosed strategy shifts, un-made decisions, parallel duplicate projects, last-minute reversals of completed work, and goals that were never truly aligned. Her central argument is that change is unavoidable but whiplash is manufactured — it is what happens when change occurs without communication. She offers two practical rules: feel like a broken record (repetition is what it takes for communication to actually land), and always craft messages for the newest, most junior person with the least context. She concludes that clear delegation, with one person owning each initiative and a defined path to decision, is unglamorous but essential to preventing wasted time and burned-out talent.
points: "Work whiplash" is distinct from hard work — it is the experience of effort rendered meaningless by undisclosed changes in direction, signaling to high performers that their time does not matter and leading them to stop running hard.

The gap between what leadership knows and what employees know is the manufacturing plant for whiplash; the remedy is treating "who needs to know about this?" as a non-optional follow-up question every time a decision shifts.

Once a company passes 50 employees, the default assumption must flip from "people know" to "people do not know" — and effective communication requires a near-insane level of repetition to even approach actual comprehension.

Clear delegation — one owner per initiative, a defined decision-making path, an agreed timeline — is boring and essential; without it, people do enormous amounts of work that goes nowhere because they never knew who could say yes.

Graham's sharpest practical rule: always craft communications for the person who started this week — the most junior employee with the least context — because that is the bar at which organizational communication actually becomes communication.
quotes: Nothing burns great people out faster than what I call work whiplash. People can handle hard work. They struggle when priorities constantly reverse, decisions get made and un-made, and goals keep changing underneath them.

One of the most demoralizing things that can happen to someone at work is spending weeks pushing something uphill only to find out the strategy changed, the project no longer matters, or another team was quietly working on the same thing on the other side of the building.

I think leaders often underestimate how emotionally exhausting this is for their teams. You are holding context that your team does not have. You are in rooms they are not in. Decisions get made at the leadership level that feel small or obvious to you and land as earthquakes on the people executing underneath you.
Change is inevitable. Whiplash is not. Whiplash is what happens when change occurs without communication.

The gap between what leadership knows and what everyone else knows is where most work whiplash gets manufactured. And the only thing that closes that gap is treating who needs to know about this as a non-optional follow-up question every time a decision gets made or a priority shifts.

Work whiplash is, at its core, wasted time. When you hire someone, you are fundamentally paying for their time and their skills. Nothing should concern companies more than wasted time, and yet so much of it is wasted by bad process, bad leadership, and bad structure.

Clear delegation — one person who owns something, a handful of people who need to weigh in, an agreed-upon timeline — sounds incredibly boring. It is boring. It also prevents an enormous amount of wasted time and burned-out talent.
